newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - When Nemesis beckoned the market mavericks.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - When Nemesis beckoned the market mavericks.

text.p: Fate turned sour in 1996 for the rogue trader.

Scarcely had Nick Leeson begun a jail term after he broke Britain's blueblood Barings bank, with a clientele that included Queen Elizabeth, than prosecutors were knocking on the suburban Tokyo door of Yasuo Hamanaka.
Japan's disgraced mastermind of the murky, London-based world trade in copper is alleged to have lost his employer, Sumitomo Corp, an epic $2.6 billion or almost twice what Leeson cost Barings.
As Hamanaka faced charges of fraud and forgery, pundits differ on whether coming months may uncover yet other scandals of such historic dimension and on the scale of malpractice.
But government regulators drew comfort from the way that, if open to abuse, the late 20th century's free-wheeling financial markets have not yet collapsed under this kind of shock.

Sumitomo, a huge metals conglomerate, absorbed the Hamanaka hit. It arranged to unload his exposed positions in copper in a repair job as swift as the 1995 takeover by Dutch bank ING, under the watchful eye of the central banks, of stricken Barings.
COPPER DOWN BUT NOT OUT

Copper prices fell but they weren't destroyed. At around $2,000 per tonne they are only some 25 per cent below a cyclical peak to which a technical squeeze, exerted by Hamanaka, had driven them back in May.
A view strengthened that regulators and companies had learned their lessons, supervision was tightening and techniques of crisis management had been honed.
"There's been no domino effect, no spillovers into other markets or system meltdown," said Charles Hatton at brokerage E D and F Man.
Hatton presented a study of the rogue trader phenomenon during this year's London Metal Exchange (LME) trade week.
It reviewed other recent losses on derivative investment instruments, including $1.3 billion at Metallgesellschaft in 1993.
There were also $1.1 billion on bonds at Daiwa Bank that, like Hamanaka's losses, were said to have been concealed.
Hatton also posed possibly the biggest unanswered question in the Sumitomo affair, that may be aired when Hamanaka comes to court, which is how far he really was a lone maverick.
By Sumitomo's account, he lost the $2.6 billion in rogue trades that he began 10 years ago to cover a loss of just $59 million.
The firm says the business was conducted off the books, involved forged and destroyed documents and, most importantly, the key player acted completely alone.

"On the other hand," Hatton added, "If one condensed the press reports...the case looks like one of global conspiracy permitted by regulatory lassitude and aided by a troop of physical agents and friendly...brokers and funded by generous derivatives-linked bank loans".
BIG EGO MARKS ROGUE TRADER

Hatton drew on psychological studies to portray the character of a rogue trader as, typically, a man with a big ego who covers up a mistake to save face and then is driven to despair as an audit closes in.
Singapore-based Leeson seemed to step straight from central casting for the role of dealing room high flier. Fellow patrons of fashionable Harry's Bar knew him as "Lucky" Nick.

Just 28, he gambled billions in derivatives that were tied to the value of Japanese stocks, winning handsome bonuses for himself and his bosses. When the market swung against him he hid his failure in fake deals. Then he despaired.
In his book "Rogue Trader" he dubbed himself "the trading superstar who moved the market this way and that".
But Hamanaka, 20 years older than Leeson, could less easily be made to conform to the image.

A policeman's son, strap-hanging in a commuter train home to suburban Kawasaki and to a wife and teenage children and weekend strolls with the family dog, he seemed the model of a loyal, self-effacing Tokyo "salary man".

Yet, for a decade, he had outfoxed a multitrillion-dollar market, winning citations from Sumitomo as the star trader who dovetailed a lucrative trade in derivatives with a corporate strategy to control 20 percent of world copper.
His trades, done with sophisticated Western brokers and in volume of almost $10 billion a year, apparently offset Sumitomo losses selling metal cheap in Asia in a bid for market share.
FRAUD SQUADS SEEK OUT CORRUPTION

Late in 1996, the British Securities and Investments Board (SIB) fine-tuned reforms, under post-Sumitomo pressure to make the London trade in metals more transparent and to regulate off-market deals done outside the London Metal Exchange.

Separately, fraud squads on three continents sifted the evidence in case it was a wider web of corruption, rather than just a lack of supervision of this over-the-counter business, that had entangled and ruined aspiring traders from Asia and elsewhere.
Their bottom line was that Hamanaka wasn't alone in seeing the inside of a prison cell in connection with metals trading centred on London.
Jailed in China was Chen Tongsheng. He was alleged to have lost $40 million in 1994 on unauthorized metals deals for the China International Trust and Investment Corp.

Let out of prison in Chile, because he has cancer, was Juan Pablo Davila, 37. Convicted of tax evasion but denying fraud, he has been blamed for alleged maverick deals that lost the Chilean state copper company Codelco $175 million.
